name: Ivan Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Ivan. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me is confidential. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Depends on the season, that's the first thing. Right now, in November, I'm drilling the last of the winter wheat on Brookfield Estate, so I'm in the cab of the big green tractor by seven and I might not get out till dark except to fill up the drill. In spring it's lambing with the 900 ewes, which is the opposite, all hands and no sleep. I like the cab work more than I let on, with the radio and the gulls following the drill.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me a bit about the estate and your life outside it.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It's about 600 hectares, wheat, oilseed rape, beans and the sheep, owned by a family who live abroad mostly, run by a farm manager called Claire. There are four of us full-time. I share a house in Marston with my cousin Kwame and a friend from college, so rent's cheap, and I've got about three months of money put by. No partner right now, which my mum mentions every Sunday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fair enough, it's a tool like the GPS steering was. When the auto-steer came in, everyone said tractor drivers were done, and here I still am, just with straighter lines. I'd probably post something like that, a bit of a joke.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be pleased, because it means the thing I'm good at stays worth something. I use one of those AI chat apps now and then, to work out a spray label or get the gist of a manual written in German, and that's about as far as I'd want it to go. I'd also think: good, now the estate has no excuse to not give us a pay rise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on at Brookfield, mostly. I'd keep the three months saved and try to get it to five, and maybe use the AI app a bit more for the boring stuff like the spray records. I'd also ask Claire about the sprayer operator's ticket, the higher one, because that pays a bit more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's the version where I get to just get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a pay rise. Do you think a plateau would help the workers or the owners more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The owners, if I'm honest. Even a small bit of time saved ends up in their pocket, because nobody's going to pay me extra for the hour the computer saved Claire. That's why I think there should be a proper union deal for farm staff, not just whatever each farm feels like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a really good day in the cab look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A dry October day, soil just right, the drill going in clean, and you look back at the end and there's forty hectares done with no gaps. Nobody sees it but you and the crows. Then a couple of weeks later it greens up in rows and you think, I did that.

S0.say: I'd say it's a tool, like GPS steering was. When auto-steer came in everyone said tractor drivers were done, and I'm still here, just with straighter lines.
S0.think: I'd be pleased, because what I'm good at stays worth something and I only want AI for things like reading a spray label. I'd also think the estate has no excuse left for not giving us a pay rise.
S0.do: Keeps working at Brookfield Estate and tries to build his savings from three months to five. Uses the AI app a little more for spray records and asks the farm manager about the higher sprayer operator's certificate for extra pay.
S0.feel: Calm. This is the version where he gets to carry on.
S0.quote: When the auto-steer came in, everyone said tractor drivers were done, and here I still am, just with straighter lines.
S0.fieldNote: Ivan is relaxed and quietly proud of his cab work. Even in the calmest picture he notices who keeps the gains, and he wants a proper agreement on farm pay rather than each farm deciding alone. His description of a good drilling day was one of the most vivid moments of the interview.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is what happened with GPS, but bigger, so let's make sure the workers get trained and not just dropped. I'd bring it up with the others at break and say we should be asking Claire now what the plan is. Online I'd share stuff about training grants and the farmworkers' union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think tractor driving is in trouble. There's already a driverless tractor being trialled on a big farm in the next county, and once those are proven, a place like Brookfield would have one in five years. I'm not worried about the sheep yet, because lambing is messy, but most of my winter is in that cab.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the union properly in the first month, which I've meant to do for years. Then I'd wait until the robot kit was actually working on farms near us, and once it was, I'd ask the estate to send me on whatever course the dealer runs for setting up and fixing them. Meanwhile, I'd save, maybe a hundred a month more by skipping the new phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not scared. It feels like something I can get in front of if I'm sensible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait until it's proven. What would count as proven, for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When I see it on a farm like ours, with hedges and wet corners and a manager who swears at it, and it still works. Not on a demonstration field at a show. If Dev at Highfield Farm got one and it ran a whole season, I'd be convinced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about on the estate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pete, the stockman, maybe not, because the sheep keep him safe. It's Ali I'd worry about, who's sixty and only drives. He can't read well and he gets by because he knows the land by heart. Nobody's going to send him on a computer course.

S1.say: I'd say this is GPS again but bigger, so workers should be trained, not dropped. I'd ask the others to push the manager for a plan and share news about training grants and the union.
S1.think: I think tractor driving is in trouble, because driverless tractors are already being trialled nearby. The sheep work feels safer, but most of my winter is in that cab.
S1.do: Joins the union properly in the first month and saves about a hundred a month more by skipping a new phone. Waits until robot machinery is proven on a farm like his, then asks the estate to send him on the dealer's course for setting up and repairing it.
S1.feel: Uneasy but not scared. He feels he can get ahead of it if he's sensible.
S1.quote: When I see it on a farm like ours, with hedges and wet corners and a manager who swears at it, and it still works.
S1.fieldNote: Ivan's steadiness shows in his clear test for when he'd move: proof on a real farm, not a show field. He sees risk to his own cab work honestly, yet his biggest concern is for an older colleague who can't read well. His progressive views come out as training and union membership rather than anger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast and someone has to slow it down, the government, whoever. You can't let a few companies switch off half the jobs in the country in two years. I'd be backing anyone calling for a basic income, money paid to everyone, because what else is there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd lose the job, and the estate would be the first to go for it, because the owners aren't even here to see who they're letting go. But I'm twenty-seven, single, living in a house share. I'm not the one who'd be hit hardest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut back to basics straight away and keep every penny of the three months. I'd talk to the union about what we can get from the estate when the cuts come, like a decent pay-off. If the job went, I'd probably move back to my parents' in town for a bit, help my dad in his shop, and look for whatever's still done by hand, maybe on a smaller farm that can't afford the machines yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Tight in the chest. But I keep coming back to the fact that I've got nobody depending on me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep saying you're not the one hit hardest. Is that true, or is it what you tell yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bit of both, probably. I'd still be twenty-nine with no job and back in my old bedroom with the football posters. But I can see Ali, and the families with kids at school, and it'd feel wrong to make it about me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum on the Sunday call?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her it's fine, I've got some money, I'll come back for a bit. She'd say she always wanted me home anyway. And then she'd ask if I'd met anyone, because that's how my mum handles a crisis.

S2.say: I'd say it's too fast and somebody, the government or whoever, has to slow it down. I'd back calls for a basic income, money paid to everyone, because I can't see what else would work.
S2.think: I think I'd lose the job, and an owner who lives abroad wouldn't think twice. But I'm twenty-seven, single and in a house share, so I'm not the one who'd be hit hardest.
S2.do: Cuts back to basics and protects his three months of savings. Works with the union to get a decent pay-off from the estate, and if the job goes, moves back to his parents, helps in his father's shop and looks for hand work on smaller farms.
S2.feel: Anxious and tight in the chest, but steadied by having nobody depending on him.
S2.quote: I'd still be twenty-nine with no job and back in my old bedroom with the football posters.
S2.fieldNote: Ivan copes with the fast scenario by comparing himself to people with more to lose, and he admitted that this is partly a story he tells himself. His plan leans on family and on getting a fair pay-off through the union. He expects an absent owner to cut staff quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to plan this one properly, so let's not waste it. I'd be pushing for colleges to run courses for farm workers on the new machines, paid by the companies selling them. At work I'd say to the others, we've got about three years to get on the right side of this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it's about the right amount of time for me. I'd be thirty-two when it arrives, and if I've learned to set up and fix the machines by then, I might be one of the few people a big farm still needs. If I wait too long, that door shuts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch for a year, see who's buying what. By the second year, once the kit was clearly working round here, I'd sign up for an agricultural engineering course at the college, evenings or day release, and start using AI tools more to plan the work. I'd save hard, maybe get to six months, so I could take a cut in pay to do an apprenticeship-type job with a dealer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but with a plan. It feels like a job I'd have to get done, more than a disaster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Even the people who fix the machines might be replaced by 2031. Does that change your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, I've thought about that. Someone's still got to drive out to a field at six in the morning when the thing's stuck in a ditch. Maybe that lasts five years, maybe ten. It's not forever, but nothing is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be giving up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The cab, the quiet, the drilling days. I'd be in a van going from farm to farm with a laptop, fixing other people's robots. It'd pay better, probably, but I'd miss looking back at a field I'd done.

S3.say: I'd say there's time to plan this one properly, so let's not waste it. I'd push for college courses on the new machines for farm workers, paid for by the companies selling them.
S3.think: Five years is about the right amount of time for me. If I've learned to set up and fix the machines by thirty-two, I might be one of the few people a big farm still needs, but if I wait too long that door shuts.
S3.do: Watches the first year to see what local farms buy, then signs up for an agricultural engineering course in the second year and uses AI tools more to plan work. Saves towards six months so he can take a pay cut for a training job with a machinery dealer.
S3.feel: Uneasy but with a plan. It feels like a job to get done more than a disaster.
S3.quote: I'd be in a van going from farm to farm with a laptop, fixing other people's robots.
S3.fieldNote: Five years matches Ivan's style exactly: a year to watch, then a firm move. He knows even repair work may not last but accepts that nothing is permanent. What he would mourn is the satisfaction of finishing a field himself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, as long as governments use it. I'd want a plan for rural areas in particular, because the cities always get the help first. I'd be telling people at the young farmers' club to start thinking now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the ten-year one is almost harder for me, because I'd keep putting it off. I'm the type who waits until it's proven, and with ten years it'd always feel like there's time. I could easily be thirty-five and still in the cab, telling myself next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd give myself a deadline, maybe written on the calendar: by thirty, have a second skill. Probably the engineering course, maybe electrics. I'd keep driving at Brookfield, save steadily, and maybe look at sharing a house purchase with Kwame, because a place of our own would be one less bill if work went.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, quietly. Not frightened, more like a nagging that I'd have to keep listening to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why buying a house, of all things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because rent's the thing that would kill us if wages went. If Kwame and I had a small place paid off, or mostly, we could ride out a bad few years. My dad did that with his shop, he owns the building, and it saved him more than once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the difference, for you, between two years and ten?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two I'm reacting, scrambling. With ten I'm the one deciding, if I've got the guts to actually do it. The danger is that I don't.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty if governments use it, with a proper plan for rural areas, because cities always get help first. I'd tell people at the young farmers' club to start thinking now.
S4.think: The ten-year picture is almost harder for me, because I'm someone who waits for proof and I'd keep putting it off. I could be thirty-five and still in the cab, telling myself next year.
S4.do: Sets himself a deadline of having a second skill by thirty, probably agricultural engineering or electrics, while still driving at Brookfield. Saves steadily and looks at buying a small house with his cousin to cut rent risk.
S4.feel: Quietly uneasy, like a nagging he would have to keep listening to.
S4.quote: I could easily be thirty-five and still in the cab, telling myself next year.
S4.fieldNote: Ivan sees that his own caution is the main risk in the slow scenario, and he'd guard against it with a written deadline. His idea of buying a house with his cousin comes from watching his father own his shop building. The difference he draws between reacting and deciding was clear and personal.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most for everyone else, and the ten-year one worries me for me, if that makes sense. What would help is paid training that comes to rural places, run through colleges, and a union deal so farm staff get warning and a fair pay-off. And honestly, someone checking in on people like Ali.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe who owns the robots. If the estate owns them, the money goes abroad with the owners. If farmers' co-ops or the village owned them, at least some of it would stay here. I don't know how you'd do that, but it's the question nobody asks.

headlineQuote: With two I'm reacting, scrambling. With ten I'm the one deciding, if I've got the guts to actually do it.
portrait: Ivan Mensah is 27 and drives tractors and helps with 900 ewes on Brookfield Estate, a 600-hectare farm owned by a family who mostly live abroad. He shares a cheap house with his cousin, has about three months saved, and uses AI apps now and then for spray labels and manuals. He wants proof before he moves, and his test is a robot working on a real farm with hedges and wet corners. The fast scenario makes him anxious, but he steadies himself by thinking of colleagues with more to lose. With five or ten years he plans to retrain in machine repair, while worrying that a long warning would let him put it off.
biggestWorry: AGI in two years worries him most for other people, while the ten-year version worries him for himself because he might keep putting off change.
whatWouldHelp: Paid training brought to rural areas through colleges, a union agreement giving farm staff warning and a fair pay-off, and someone checking on older workers.
